title: Drift or Selection? On Your Own
subject: biology
instructions: Answer on your own, even though you ran populations with your group. Write your ID number, not your name.

questions.skill: I can find an allele frequency
questions.prompt: Frequency: A population has 7 A copies and 13 a copies. What fraction of the copies are A? Give a decimal.
questions.key: 7 ÷ (7 + 13) = 7 ÷ 20 = 0.35. Look for 0.54 (7 ÷ 13, A over a instead of over the total).

questions.prompt: Lost by Chance: In a drift-only cup, nothing made A better or worse, yet after 8 generations every copy was a. Why?

options.text: The a copies were better adapted.
options.why: Nothing favored a: survival was the same for both.

options.text: By chance, some A copies weren't passed on, and once A was gone it couldn't come back.
options.why: Yes: random sampling, generation after generation.

options.text: The A copies changed into a copies.
options.why: No copy changed; some just weren't drawn.

options.text: The population was too large to keep both.

questions.prompt: Size Matters: Which population is most likely to lose a gene version by chance alone in 10 generations?

options.why: Yes: small samples swing the most.
Bigger samples stay closer to the start.
Chance swings shrink as populations grow.

questions.skill: I can tell drift from selection
questions.prompt: Drift or Selection? Two small populations both ended all A. In one, A copies survived better; in the other, nothing favored either. How could scientists tell which was selection? Use what the class's cups showed.

rubric.criterion: Repeats: says to look at many populations (or repeat it), not just one.
Selection: says selection pushes most populations the same way (toward A).
Drift: says drift goes either way at random (some lose A, some lose a).
